modules.title: Meaning, Features, and Process of Communication
text: Core Concept: Communication is sharing information among people to reach a common understanding.

Skill Classification: It is called a soft skill (unlike technical or domain-based "hard skills") and is vital because business executives spend most of their time communicating to build favourable relationships.
Newman and Summer: "Communication is an exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or emotions by two or more persons.".
Allen Louis: "It is the sum of all the things one person does when he wants to create an understanding in the mind of another.".
Hoben: "The verbal interchange of thoughts or ideas.".
Anderson: "The process by which we understand others and in turn, endeavour to be understood by them; It is dynamic, constantly changing and shifting in response to the total situation.".
Berelson and Steiner: "The transmission of information, ideas, emotions, skills, etc. by the use of symbols, words, pictures, figures, graphs, etc.".
Fotheringham: "A process involving the selection, production, and transmission of signs in such a way as to help a receiver perceive a meaning similar to that in the mind of the communicator.".
Unavoidable: You cannot avoid communicating—even silence, body language, dress, punctuality, and workplace environment send messages.
Two-Way Exchange: A continuous exchange of information and feedback between two or more people.

A Process: Messages do not happen in isolation—their meaning depends on past interactions and present context (e.g., your boss's reply to a promotion request depends on your past relationship and their current mood).
Involves a Sender and a Receiver: Starts with a sender transmitting a message and requires a receiver to attach meaning to it.
Verbal or Non-Verbal: Can happen with words (spoken/written) or without words (gestures, facial expressions); Succeeds only when the receiver understands the sender's intended meaning.
Dynamic Process: Constantly adapts in mode and manner depending on the situation while assimilating, processing, and responding.
Enables Understanding: Helps people understand why change is needed, how to carry out processes, and why their actions matter.
Sender (Encoder): The person who creates and sends the message (e.g., a manager writing a letter or giving a sales presentation).
Message: Any signal that triggers a response—can be intentional (a presentation) or unintentional (yawning showing boredom).
Channel: The medium/method used to deliver the message (letter, email, telephone, speech).
Receiver (Decoder): The person who receives and interprets the message (misinterpretation can happen—e.g., a friendly joke taken as an insult, or constructive feedback taken as negative criticism).

Feedback: The receiver's response to the message—can be oral (asking questions), written (replying to a complaint), non-verbal (nods and smiles), or even silence/no response (showing lack of interest); Because of feedback, people in face-to-face talks are simultaneously senders and receivers.

Context: The setting in which communication occurs, classified into four types:; Physical Context: Physical surroundings (asking for a promotion in your office vs boss's office vs a company party vs over lunch).; Social Context: Relationship between sender and receiver (how well you get along with your boss).; Chronological Context: Time-related factors (morning vs end of day; work hours vs after hours; during profits vs during a factory strike or losses).; Cultural Context: Background similarities/differences such as age, language, nationality, religion, and gender.
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Sent by the wrong person (e.g., a junior accountant writing to a bank for a multi- crore project loan).
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Unclear/badly worded message or too many messages causing information overload.
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Wrong channel chosen (e.g., placing a liquor ad in a religious magazine).
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Wrong interpretation by the receiver or inadequate feedback.
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Physical, physiological, or psychological noise distorting the message.
Communication Process and Key Elements: When Communication Can Go Wrong
Wrong physical, social, chronological, or cultural context.

modules.title: Types of Communication (Verbal & Non-Verbal)
text: Communication is broadly divided into two types: Verbal Communication (using words) and Non-Verbal Communication (without words).
Verbal communication uses words to convey thoughts and includes two forms:
Oral Communication: Spoken interaction to influence listeners (meetings, presentations, one-to-one talks, performance appraisals, talking, laughing, listening).
Written Communication: Handwritten, printed, or typed correspondence (letters, memos, circulars, notices, reports, emails, scripts, acronyms, logos, graphics).
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
Message relates directly or indirectly to an object; uses concepts; content must be understood by both sender and receiver; influenced by cultural factors and the sender's emotional state of mind.
Verbal Communication: Four Levels of Verbal Communication
Intrapersonal Communication: Private self-talk—organising your own thoughts to build clarity and confidence before speaking to others.
Verbal Communication: Four Levels of Verbal Communication
Interpersonal Communication: One-to-one communication between two people— requires active listening, thinking before replying, and reading cues.
Verbal Communication: Four Levels of Verbal Communication
Group Communication: Small group discussions (team meetings, board meetings, sales meetings) where everyone can interact and stay on topic.
Verbal Communication: Four Levels of Verbal Communication
Public / Mass Communication: Public speaking where one speaker addresses a large audience (speeches, election campaigns, large presentations)—needs simple language, structure, and preparation.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication
General Benefits: Complete understanding with room to clarify; fast and time- efficient; allows immediate feedback; enables persuasion and influence; flexible in tone and language.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication

Five Benefits for Professionals: a; Building relationships & teamwork. b; Persuading co-workers/stakeholders. c; Bringing clarity by repeating/explaining during conflicts. d; Improving productivity through collaboration. e; Increasing motivation via appreciation and supportive feedback.
Non-verbal communication conveys meaning without words or sounds (e.g., the game of "Dumb Charades").

Often has more impact than words ("how you say something" matters more than "what you say"). Example: A boss asks for your improvement ideas, but yawns, slouches, frowns, looks out the window, and gives an angry "thank you" with a curt handshake—clearly signalling he does not care despite his polite words.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication
Cannot be avoided: Even silence or refusing to speak sends a message (e.g., an audience staying silent and yawning sends negative feedback).
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication
Powerful: Shapes lasting first impressions (e.g., arriving 15 minutes late to an interview in casual clothes and avoiding eye contact creates a poor impression).
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication
Ambiguous: Not always clear—slouching could mean boredom or fatigue; avoiding eye contact could mean nervousness or guilt.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication
Cannot express all messages: Expresses feelings, attitudes, and interest, but complex facts/numbers (like exceeding annual sales targets) require spoken or written words.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Varies across cultures: Physical contact/handshakes are common in Western cultures but viewed as intimate in Oriental cultures like India; nodding means yes in some cultures and no in others; bowing shows respect in Japan but is unusual in the USA; prolonged eye contact shows interest/trustworthiness in Arab cultures but is avoided in Latin America and parts of Asia/Africa; Latin Americans stand close while Westerners prefer distance.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Kinesics - Description: Body language & movements; Key Details & Examples: Facial expressions (happiness, anger, sadness), eye movements/contact, gestures (hand movements show involvement; shuffling feet = nervousness; hands in pockets = casual/rude), head nods, posture (erect = attentive; crossed arms = defensive), physical appearance/dress code.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Haptics - Description: Communication through touch; Key Details & Examples: Used for working (doctors, security), greeting (handshakes, embraces), friendship (friendly pat), guiding, and managing interactions; Must be used carefully as it varies by culture (less touch in Asian,.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Proxemics - Description: Personal space and distance; Key Details & Examples: Intimate space (family/close friends), Personal space (friends/colleagues), Social & Public space (formal workplace); Workplace also uses Fixed space (permanent furniture/rooms → formality) and Semi-fixed space (movable seating → informality); Space can signal leadership positions.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Chronemics - Description: Use of time & punctuality; Key Details & Examples: Attitudes toward punctuality and waiting; Western cultures treat punctuality strictly; arriving early shows seriousness; spending time coaching staff shows care.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Paralanguage - Description: Tone of voice ("how" you say it); Key Details & Examples: Closest to verbal communication; Includes pitch (high/low), pace (fast/ slow), volume (soft/loud), and word emphasis (stressing "I" vs "good business communication" changes meaning); Avoid mixed signals.
Non-Verbal Communication: Five Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication

Physical Context - Description: Physical environment & surroundings; Key Details & Examples: Colours (black/grey = mourning/negative; yellow/ green = positive feelings), office layout & design (executive chair, carpet = status/formality), space management, location (city business district = success vs suburbs), and physical distance (requiring video calls/emails).

modules.title: Communication Models & Barriers to Communication
text: David Berlo's SMCR Model of Communication (1960)
Proposed by David K. Berlo in 1960; views communication as four interacting components: Source → Message → Channel → Receiver (SMCR).
David Berlo's SMCR Model of Communication (1960)
Source (Sender): Initiates communication; effectiveness depends on the sender's communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, and cultural background.
David Berlo's SMCR Model of Communication (1960)
Message: The information/idea conveyed; includes content (actual info), structure (organisation), code, and treatment (e.g., a presentation using charts and examples).
David Berlo's SMCR Model of Communication (1960)

Channel: Medium carrying the message—Berlo highlighted the five sensory channels (hearing, seeing, touching, smelling, tasting); In business: meetings, emails, phone calls, reports, video presentations (visual + auditory).
David Berlo's SMCR Model of Communication (1960)

Receiver: Interprets the message; influenced by the same factors as the source (skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, culture); Core Lesson: Communication succeeds when sender and receiver share similar understanding and use appropriate channels.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication (1949)
Known as the "Mathematical Model of Communication," designed for electronic media.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication (1949)

Five Core Components (+ Noise & Feedback): a. Information Source (Sender): Generates the desired message. b. Transmitter (Encoder): Converts the message into signals for transmission. c. Channel: Path carrying signals to the receiver (where Noise—unwanted disturbances like radio static or phone noise—can enter). d. Receiver (Decoder): Inverse transmitter that converts signals back into a message. e. Destination: The final consumer of the message.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication (1949)

Three Levels of Communication Challenges Identified:; Technical issues: Reliability of signal transfer.; Semantic issues: Whether the receiver interprets the sender's intended meaning accurately.; Influential (Effectiveness) issues: Whether the message achieves the desired behaviour from the receiver.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication (1949)

Key Critique & Insight: Originally a linear, one-way model placing little focus on feedback; Shows that reducing noise, increasing bandwidth, enhancing signal strength, and improving encoding/decoding reduce uncertainty.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Physical Noise: Distracting sounds, poor acoustics, or information overload.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Physiological Noise: Hearing/physical disabilities, fatigue, or illness affecting speaking/listening.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Psychological Noise: Emotions inside sender or receiver—preoccupations, hostility, fear, or lack of interest (e.g., not listening to a professor because you think they have nothing new to say).
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Environmental Barriers: Same as physical noise: distracting sounds, overcrowded room, poor facilities/acoustics.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Individual Barriers: Tendency to judge, evaluate, approve, or disapprove of another's views—especially when holding strong feelings—blocking out the message.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise

Organisational Barriers: (a) Multiple hierarchical layers distorting a message as it passes down (e.g., Halley's Comet memo from Space Centre Chief → Director → Executive Directors → HODs → Managers → Executives got twisted into "Tomorrow at 20:00 hrs our Chief will disappear!"); (b) Departmental barriers where departments work in isolation with no coordination.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Channel Barriers: Choosing the wrong medium (e.g., conveying formal rules orally instead of in writing, or sending sensitive emotional feedback in writing instead of orally).
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise

Linguistic & Cultural Barriers: Using an unfamiliar foreign language, overly technical jargon, or literal cross-cultural translations (e.g., Pepsi's "Come Alive with Pepsi" translated into Chinese as "Pepsi brings your ancestors back from the grave!"), plus differing cultural values/ perceptions.
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Semantic Barriers: Differences in word meanings across cultures/contexts (e.g., "went like a bomb" means huge success in British English, whereas "bombed" means disaster in American English).
Types of Noise & Seven Barriers to Communication: Three Types of Noise
Non-Verbal Barriers: Negative tone of voice or conflicting body language undermining positive words (e.g., saying "I am delighted to meet you" in a sad tone).

modules.title: Business Communication & Corporate Communication
text: Concept and Importance of Business Communication

Concept: The structured, goal-oriented exchange of information, ideas, and messages within (internal) and outside (external) an organisation to achieve professional objectives—using oral, written, visual, and digital channels.
Concept and Importance of Business Communication

Importance of Business Communication: a. Coordination & Productivity: Clarifies roles, tasks, and deadlines so teams work efficiently. b. Informed Decision-Making: Supplies managers with timely reports, data, and feedback. c. Building Professional Relationships: Builds trust between managers and staff, and credibility with customers and partners. d. Conflict Management & Problem-Solving: Open discussion resolves misunderstandings before they escalate. e. Reputation & Brand Image: Advertisements, press releases, and social media shape public perception.

Superiors (Higher-ups) - Appropriate Channel(s): Written reports (daily/weekly sales); Presentations; One-to- one face-to-face meetings (best for solving problems); Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Awareness of progress, sharing suggestions/ feedback, and problem- solving.

Peers (Co-workers at same level, e.g., Marketing & HR Managers) - Appropriate Channel(s): Oral face-to-face meetings (best for building rapport); Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Functional coordination (e.g., approving ad budget with Finance), teamwork, and information sharing.

Subordinates (People reporting to you) - Appropriate Channel(s): Written communication (for policies/procedures); Oral face-to-face meetings (for appraisals/feedback); Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Compliance with instructions and policies, reviewing progress, performance feedback, rewards, discipline.

Employees / Unions - Appropriate Channel(s): Written communication (written contracts kept on record); Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Employee satisfaction and welfare, clear terms of employment, and disciplinary rules.

Shareholders (Owners of the company) - Appropriate Channel(s): Oral & written: Meetings, conferences, letters, brochures, advertisements; Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Building trust and confidence; transparent updates on progress, new projects, capital issues, and major problems.

Enhance Credit Rating: Good external communication strengthens borrowing capacity for expansion.

Consumers - Appropriate Channel(s): Written: Advertisements (mass media), letters; Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Awareness, product/offer information, persuasion, and redressing complaints.

Intermediaries (Distributors, wholesalers, retailers, franchisees) - Appropriate Channel(s): Written contracts, dealer newsletters, ads; Oral review meetings & sales staff; Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Awareness, product availability/order info, and motivation through incentives/ competitions.

Suppliers (Raw materials, components, utilities) - Appropriate Channel(s): Direct oral face-to-face communication; Online B2B channels; Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Ongoing relationship and partnership, clear technical specifications, quality, and timely delivery.

Government - Appropriate Channel(s): Formal written letters (for clearances/licences); Periodic meetings; Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Government cooperation, tax/ legal compliance, clearances for joint ventures, foreign borrowing, and forex.

Media - Appropriate Channel(s): Press/news conferences (oral); News/press releases and letters (written); Primary Objective(s) & Key Notes: Maintaining good relations to earn credible free publicity and protect institutional image.

modules.title: Introduction
text: Communication is an important component of success in our personal and professional lives. It is the key to building favourable relationships. It is referred to as ‘soft skill,' as opposed to domain-based or technical knowledge skills, which fall under the category of ‘hard skills.’ A formal study of business communication is important because a business executive needs to invest most of his time in communicating with various people for multiple reasons.. In this unit, we will discuss how communication involves certain key elements suitable and required for every context related to business organisation.. We will also focus on the types of communication, importance of business communication, and the different types of corporate communication in organisations.

modules.title: Communication – Meaning And Definition
text: Communication, in simple terms, is sharing of information among people, to reach/ achieve a platform of a common understanding.
Communication has been defined differently by different writers and behavioural theorists.
Let’s look at some popular definitions of communication:
According to Newman and Summer, “Communication is an exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or emotions by two or more persons”.
According to Allen Louis, “It is the sum of all the things one person does when he wants to create an understanding in the mind of another”.
Hoben defines communication as “The verbal interchange of thoughts or ideas”.

In the words of Anderson, “Communication is the process by which we understand others and in turn, endeavour to be understood by them. It is dynamic, constantly changing and shifting in response to the total situation”.
According to Berelson and Steiner, “Communication is the transmission of information, ideas, emotions, skills, etc. by the use of symbols, words, pictures, figures, graphs, etc.”.

In the words of Fotheringham, “Communication is a process involving the selection, production, and transmission of signs in such a way as to help a receiver perceive a meaning similar to that in the mind of the communicator”.
From all these definitions, it can be concluded that communication has the following characteristic features:

It is unavoidable – It is impossible to avoid communication, as through our silence or body movements we even unintentionally end up communicating with others. Our body language, the way we dress, the importance we place on arriving on time, our behaviours, and the physical environment we maintain in our workplace, all convey certain messages to others.
It is a two-way exchange of information – Communication is the continuous process of exchanging information and feedback between two or more persons.

It is a process – Each message is part of a process and does not occur in isolation. This means that the meaning attached to a message depends on what has happened before and in the present context. For example, your boss’s response to your request for a promotion will depend on your past relationship with him, as well as his mood at that moment.
It involves a sender and a receiver – Any communication starts with a sender of a message and requires a receiver to attach some meaning to that message.

It could be verbal or non-verbal – Communication can happen with or without t words. body language such as gestures and facial expressions are part of communication. It can also take place in spoken or written form, It is successful when the receiver correctly interprets the intended meaning of the message sent by the sender. The receiver may not always attach the same meaning to a message as the sender. When the message is wrongly interpreted, the communicationfails. It is a dynamic process – Communication involves sharing of thoughts and experiences in a meaningful manner while assimilating, processing, and responding to the person one is talking with. The mode and manner of communication may vary according to the situation.

It enables understanding – Communication enables people to understand the necessity for change, the reasons for performing certain things, the method of implementing processes, and the importance of their actions.

modules.title: Communication Process And Key Elements
text: Let us now look at communication as a process and discuss its key elements.

Irrespective of the setting in which communication takes place or the number of people that are involved, all communication consists of certain key elements. The communication model shown in the figure illustrates each of these elements.
The elements involved in communication are:

Sender or encoder – The sender is the person who delivers a message. For instance, a manager writing a letter to a consultant after a meeting, or a sales manager giving a presentation to the sales team. In both cases, the manager is the sender. Receiver or decoder – The receiver is the person who perceives and interprets the meaning of the sent message. However, decoding is not always accurate, and the intended meaning may be misunderstood. For example, a friendly joke might be taken as an insult, or feedback from a superior to a subordinate might be misinterpreted as a negative criticism. Message – This is any signal that triggers the response of a receiver. Messages may be intentional (as in the example of the sales presentation by a manager to the sales team) or unintentional (non-verbal signals such as yawns that convey the message of boredom).

Channel – This refers to the medium or the method used to deliver the message. As a business executive, you will often have a choice of channels. For example, you could communicate with a customer through a letter, email or telephone.

Feedback – Most communication is two-way. Receivers generally respond to messages. For example, students may ask questions during a lecture session, and an employer may tell an employee that he has to think about his proposal. This response to a sender’s message is called feedback. This kind of feedback is oral. Sometimes feedback can also be given in written form. For example, a manager can send a written response to a customer’s letter of complaint. At other times, feedback could be non- verbal, as in smiles and nods of appreciation during a talk or presentation. Even failure to respond could be considered as feedback, since it may indicate a lack of interest or indifference to the sender’s message. Due to the element of feedback, people are simultaneously senders and receivers of information in face-to-face communication.
Context – This refers to the setting in which the communication takes place and could sometimes determine the success or failure of the communication. Context can be classified as follows:

Physical context – This refers to the physical surroundings. For example, a work or social environment, in which communication takes place. Asking your boss for a promotion might be received differently, depending on whether the communication takes place in your office, your boss’ office, at a company party, or over lunch at a restaurant.

Social context – This refers to the relationship between the sender and the receiver. Taking the same example, asking for a promotion is likely to be received differently, depending on how well you get along with your boss and whether you are personal friends or not.

Cultural context – This refers to the similarity of backgrounds between the sender and the receiver, such as age, language, nationality, religion and gender. These factors could influence communication favourably or unfavourably. Each of these key elements contributes to the success of communication. In other words, communication can go wrong if any of the following scenarios happen If the message is sent by the wrong person: Communication can fail in business communication when the wrong person, not suitable for the required communication, sends the message. For example, a junior accountant in a company writing a letter to a bank, asking for a loan for a project worth several crores, is not likely to get the bank’s approval.
If The message is unclear or badly worded. There may also be too many messages, leading to confusion and information overload.
If The wrong channel of communication is chosen. Placing an ad for a liquor product in a religious magazine for example, is not likely to be received favourably.
If the message is wrongly interpreted, i.e., the receiver attaches the wrong meaning to the message.
If the he feedback is not adequate to ensure understanding.
If the Physical, physiological or psychological noise distorts the message.
If the communication takes place in the wrong physical, social, chronological, or cultural context SELF-ASSESSMENT QUESTIONS.

modules.title: Types Of Communication
text: Having discussed the process and elements of communication, let us now discuss the types of communication.
Broadly, communication may be divided into two types. They are:
Non-verbal communication Let us briefly discuss these two types of communication.

Verbal communication – This type of communication occurs with the help of words. It provides the opportunity for personal contact and a two-way flow of information. A large part of our communication, whether at work or outside, is verbal. Verbal communication may be divided into two types. They are:

Oral communication – This type of communication may be defined as a process in which a speaker verbally interacts with one or more listeners, to influence the latter’s behaviour. Oral communication in a business context can take the form of meetings, presentations, one-to-one meetings, performance reviews, etc. Example – In a business context, a manager doing the performance appraisal with an employee or a sales manager making the sales plan presentation to the sales team. In the first example, the manager may point out areas for improvement, and in the second case, the sales manager may explain how to achieve new sales targets.

Written communication – This type of communication is correspondence made in writing. It can be handwritten, printed, or typed. For example, a manager is writing a letter of apology in response to a customer’s complaint regarding poor service. Written communication at the workplace can take several forms, such as letters, memos, circulars, notices, reports, and emails.

Non-verbal communication – This type of communication may be defined as communication without words. It refers to any way of conveying meanings without the use of words and sounds. The game of ‘Dumb Charades’ is a perfect example. Unlike verbal communication, non-verbal communication is usually unintentional. We often communicate silently, sending signals and messages through our actions as well as our words. Gestures, facial expressions, posture, and even the way we dress all contribute to non-verbal communication. Non-verbal communication can bear greater impact than verbal communication, since ‘how you say something’ is sometimes more important than ’what you say’. Although non-verbal communication can affect both our personal and business relationships, it is particularly important in the workplace. Let us consider the following scenario to understand this: Your boss has asked you to make a presentation on your suggestions for improving the organisation. You take him at his word and come prepared with an elaborate presentation and a list of ideas. However, as you make your presentation, he yawns repeatedly, sits back casually, looks out of the window, clenches his jaw muscles and begins to frown. At the end of your presentation, he rises abruptly from his chair, says ‘thank you for your ideas’ in an angry voice and gives you a curt handshake. In the given scenario, the boss, through his non-verbal behavior, conveys a message beyond the spoken words that he does not really want to listen to your suggestions. Therefore, while the spoken or written words may be perfect, the non-verbal aspects could convey the exact opposite meaning. We will discuss the different aspects of non-verbal communication in more detail at a later stage.

Verbal communication means effectively presenting your thoughts using words. Verbal communication is essential in the world of business - be it a weekly meeting or presentation to stakeholders, the importance of verbal communication is unparalleled. People always remember a person who speaks clearly, effectively, confidently, and charismatically.

Before we explore the various defining features of verbal communication, let’s look at its primary form. Verbal communication includes both oral and written communication.. Oral communication encompasses various activities such as talking, laughing or listening. We often navigate different emotional situations through oral forms of communication.
Verbal communication also includes written communication that includes scripts,, acronyms, logos and graphics.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
Several characteristics2,specific to verbal communication, arelisted below:
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
The message being communicated is directly or indirectly related to an object.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
We use concepts to communicate messages.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
The content should be understood by both the sender and receiver.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
Cultural factors influence the content of messages.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication
While communicating emotions and feelings, a sender’s state of mind influences the content of messages.
Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Verbal Communication

Even though we talk to our friends, family and coworkers regularly, we may not always be aware of how we’re communicating. Mastering the art of verbal communication will help you in more ways than one. Let’s now see different types of verbal communication.
Verbal Communication: Levels of Verbal Communication
Verbal communication can also be divided into various types such as Intrapersonal communication, Interpersonal communication, Group communication, Public or Mass communication.
Verbal Communication: Levels of Verbal Communication

Intrapersonal Communication This is your private verbal communication channel. You talk to yourself (self-talk) and articulate your thoughts. Communicating with yourself will give you more confidence and clarity in your thoughts. It’ll help you make up your mind, form your sentences, find suitable words and effective ways to connect with other people. This will help you gain the trust of your audience.
Verbal Communication: Levels of Verbal Communication

Interpersonal Communication It’s also known as one-to-one verbal communication. This type of communication happens between two individuals. It helps you understand if you’re getting your thoughts across clearly. Reactions, responses and verbal and nonverbal cues from the other person will help you understand whether you’re being understood or not. Make sure that you listen to the other person intently. Communication doesn’t just mean talking to someone. It’s also about listening. So, listen, think and then respond. Take time to think and make sure you don’t offend people with your response.
Verbal Communication: Levels of Verbal Communication

Group Communication The number of people increases in small group communication. You move from communicating with a single participant to a few more. These small groups could be team meetings, board meetings or sales meetings. The number of participants is small enough for everyone to communicate with each other. When you attend small group meetings, be prepared with a topic to make sure you stay on track. Stay on topic and allow enough time for everyone to present their thoughts.
Verbal Communication: Levels of Verbal Communication

Public/ Mass Communication It’s also known as ‘public speaking’. Here, an individual addresses a large number of people at once. Speeches, election campaigns and presentations are a few examples of public communication. Since the number of people in the audience is larger in this type of communication, be sure to use words and phrases they’ll understand easily and structure your thoughts before addressing the audience. The more prepared you are, the more confident you’ll feel like a public speaker.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication

Verbal communication is one of the most important mediums of communication. The stronger your communication skills are, the easier it is for you to establish trust and build lasting relationships with others. Here are some benefits of strong verbal communication skills:
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication
It provides a complete understanding, and there’s room to clarify any messages that may have been misunderstood.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication
It’s one of the fastest modes of communication and is time-efficient.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication
There is space for providing feedback, which allows two or more people to engage in a conversation at the same time.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication
It allows speakers to exercise influence and persuade listeners to agree with ideas, thoughts and opinions.
Verbal Communication: Advantages of Verbal Communication

It’s flexible, that is, you can change your language and tone depending on the situation you’re in, or the relationship you share with an individual In short, verbal communication is one of the most reliable methods of communication. Its benefits apply to your professional life as well. Let’s look at the various ways in which strong verbal communication skills can be beneficial for professionals.

Building relationships Verbal communication allows you to build strong interpersonal relationships. It’s easier when you find like-minded people who share similar interests, ideas and outlooks. This further encourages you to cooperate, collaborate and engage in teamwork.

Persuading someone In professional settings, you need to exert a certain amount of influence to get things going. For example, if you want your coworkers to join your project, you need to be able to convince them first. Even in brainstorming sessions, you need to be able to convince others of your ideas and perspectives.

Bringing clarity As verbal communication enables feedback, you can provide clarity to your message by repeating yourself. For example, in conflicts or arguments, you can repeat your message so that there’s no room for ambiguity.

Improving productivity With proper communication in place, you can communicate effectively with team members and people across the organisation. Well-established relationships enhance the process, allowing you to cooperate and collaborate quickly. Group discussions and teamwork maximise output, thereby increasing productivity.

Increasing motivation Verbal communication plays a crucial role in providing feedback and recognising individual effort. Whether it’s a congratulatory speech or email, words of support and appreciation boost confidence levels. Therefore, effective verbal communication opens up a two-way street that allows individuals to interact, engage and collaborate with each other, improving organisational efficiency and productivity.
We have defined non-verbal communication in the earlier part of this unit. Let us now look at t the specific features of non-verbal communication.
Non-Verbal Communication: Characteristics of Non-Verbal Communication
Here are some of its characteristics, which distinguish it from verbal communication:
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

While one can avoid verbal communication by refusing to speak or write, it is not possible to do the same with non-verbal communication. That is because non-verbal communication is not always intentional, unlike verbal messages, as pointed out earlier. Sometimes, silence itself may convey a lot of meaning.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

Example – A speaker making a presentation may find that the audience is not very interactive. Instead, he notices people yawning during his presentation. At the end of the session, when he asks for some feedback, there is total silence.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
From this example, we can say that the audience is bored with the session. The silence indicates that they have not listened to the session and that the feedback is negative.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Non-verbal communication helps us to form first impressions and make judgements of others. First impressions generally tend to be lasting impressions.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

Let us say you go for a job interview fifteen minutes late and are dressed in informal attire. When asked some questions, you avoid eye contact. This immediately reflects your attitude, and the impression formed about you is that of a person who takes things casually, is insecure and lacks knowledge.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
While precise words can be used in verbal communication to ensure that the message is clearly understood, non-verbal communication is not always clear and easy to understand.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
For example, sitting back in a relaxed posture may be a signal of boredom or fatigue. Similarly, avoiding eye contact with your audience could mean that either you are nervous or guilty of something.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Non-verbal communication cannot express all messages.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

Non-verbal behaviour can only express a person’s feelings, attitudes, level of interest, likes or dislikes for something. Certain messages about ideas or concepts can only be expressed through spoken or written words.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

Consider the following example to understand this. A sales manager wanting to report that sales for the current year have exceeded targets can only do so through a written report or oral presentation. If he is making an oral presentation, his non-verbal behaviour can only indicate how pleased he is about the increase in sales.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided

While certain types of non-verbal behaviour are universal, others may be different in different cultures. Examples – There are different rules regarding the appropriateness of the handshake in oriental and western cultures. Generally, in oriental cultures like India, any form of physical contact is not common and is interpreted as being intimate, while it is an accepted thing in Western countries.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Similarly, a nod of the head means yes in some cultures and no in other cultures.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Bowing to your superior is considered a mark of respect in Japan, but is considered unacceptable in the U.S.A.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Arabic cultures use prolonged eye contact to show their interest. But in the countries of Latin America, this is avoided.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
Businesspeople stand close together while talking in Latin American countries, butWestern countries find such closeness uncomfortable.
Non-Verbal Communication: Non-verbal communication cannot be avoided
In this age of business communication across cultures, it is important to understand these differences, especially when doing business overseas. Failure to do this could lead to costly blunders.

Let us discuss each of the aspects of non-verbal communication.

Kinesics is the most often studied and important area of non-verbal communication and refers to body movements of any kind. Different body movements can express inner states of emotion. The different body movements are:

Facial expressions – Facial expressions can convey feelings of surprise, happiness, anger and sadness. If you meet a long-lost friend and say “I am very happy to meet you again”, but with a sad facial expression, it conveys the exact opposite meaning.

Eye movements – The eye movements, such as wide-opened pupils, express feelings of surprise, excitement or even fear. The importance of eye contact with one’s audience was pointed out earlier. Direct eye contact is an indication of intensity and interest, while a lack of it can convey feelings of nervousness and guilt. Different cultures perceive eye contact differently. In Asia, Latin America and Africa, people avoid direct eye contact to show respect. Arabs use prolonged eye contact to measure trustworthiness.

Gestures – Gestures such as movement of the hands while giving a lecture or presentation indicate a high level of involvement in what you are saying. On the other hand, shuffling of the feet is a sign of nervousness and speaking with one’s hands in one’s pockets is considered to be casual or even rude.
Head movements – Movements like nodding the head can convey interest, appreciation, agreement or understanding.

Posture – Posture refers to carriage or attitude. Our posture can indicate our feelings. In formal settings such as job interviews or classroom settings, you must maintain an erect posture to convey that you are attentive, since slouching or a relaxed posture conveys a casual attitude. Similarly, crossing your arms and legs can convey that you are defensive and rigid. Uncrossing your arms and legs can indicate that you are willing to listen.

Physical appearance – Our outward appearance, including the way we dress, and present ourselves,can convey an impression of formality or informality. Going to a job interview dressed in blue jeans or not sticking to a stipulated dress code at the workplace can convey that you are a rebel, non-conformist or a very casual person.

Haptics refers to communication through touch. We can use touch to communicate affection, assurance, familiarity, comfort, sympathy and other emotions. Touching can also be interpreted as an assault. Hence, we must use touch as a communication tool carefully. Touching is used for the following purposes:
Working – Professionals such as doctors, dentists, hairdressers and airport security staff need to touch people in the normal course of their work.

Greeting – Contact through touch is part of the greeting ritual. We often use handshakes to greet people. Retaining contact for a greater duration of time can convey feelings of friendship or domination. In some cultures, people also embrace or rub noses to greet people.
Establishing friendships – A friendly pat or a comforting touch can help in establishing amicable relationships.
Guiding – A touch on the back, shoulder or arm can help guide people in the correct direction.

Managing interactions – Touching is used to manage interactions. We can gently touch the shoulder or arm to gain the attention of a person. The importance given to touch varies with culture. Asian cultures forbid displays of affection. Hence, touching is not encouraged in such cultures. Cultures, like Germany and England, that have rigid status structures and stress emotional restraint, give lesser importance to touching when compared to the countries in the Middle East and Latin America.

Proxemics is derived from the word ‘proximity’ or closeness and is the communication term for personal space and distance. The space and distance which we choose to keep from people is also part of non-verbal communication. Each of us has our own inner and outer circles, which differ for different people. The different types of spaces are as follows:
Intimate space – Our innermost circle is an ‘intimate space’, into which we generally admit only select people, such as family and close friends.
Personal space – A ‘personal space’ might include other friends and colleagues or co- workers. Intimate and personal spaces involve communication of an informal nature.

Social and public space – The ‘social and public space’ includes official or workplace relationships, where communication is of a more formal nature. In a business context, it is more relevant to understand the concept of the following spaces:
Fixed space – Fixed space means that the physical features of the work environment, such as furniture, room size and seating arrangement, are permanent. This conveys an impression of formality.

Semi-fixed space – Semi-fixed space means that certain elements of the environment can be changed. For example, changing the seating arrangement conveys an impression of informality. Space should therefore be used carefully in a work environment, so as to convey the right impressions.

Chronemics refers to the study of the usage of time. This includes our attitudes towards punctuality and willingness to wait. Perception of the importance of time varies between individuals and cultures.

For example, in most Western cultures, punctuality is considered to be important. Arriving late for a business meeting is inexcusable. In other cultures, it is more relaxed, and time is not given that much importance.

We convey messages to others through the time we spend on a work-related activity or by the importance that we give to time. Arriving early at work or for a job interview shows interest, involvement, and seriousness. Spending time with employees and giving them suggestions on how to improve their performance shows interest and involvement in their career growth.

Para means ‘like’ or ‘similar to’, therefore paralanguage means ‘like language’. Of all the forms of non-verbal communication, paralanguage is closest to verbal communication. It refers to the tone of voice with which something is said. In other words, it is ‘how’ something is said, and not ‘what’ is said. The tone of voice includes the pitch (high or low pitch), the pace (slow or fast), the emphasis on words and the volume (soft or loud) and can convey different moods and emotions.

For example, the statement, “I practice good business communication”, can be understood in different ways, depending on the emphasis on certain words. When more emphasis is given to ‘I’ while saying “I practice good business communication,” it means that the speaker alone practices it above anyone else. On the other hand, placing more emphasis on ‘practice good business communication’ could be interpreted to mean that the speaker communicates particularly well in a business context, rather than in a general context.
The important point to keep in mind regarding tone of voice is to avoid mixed signals - that is, making sure that what you say is consistent with how you say it.
Physical context refers to the physical environment or surroundings within which we communicate. This includes the following aspects:

Colour and layout – Colours are known for their symbolic meaning and have associations with different feelings. For example, colours like black and grey are associated with death, mourning and negative feelings. Yellow and green are associated with more positive feelings. Of course, these can also vary across cultures. The point to remember is that you can make the right impressions with the use of the right colours. Layout in a work environment refers to the size of an office or the arrangement of furniture.
Design – Design refers to the type of chairs, desks or carpeting. All these can convey status, formality or informality.

Space management – Space management refers to the arrangement of workspaces of people who regularly work together. It can influence employee interactions and enable effective communication. It includes the size and sequence of offices, the length and width of hallways, the arrangement of the meeting rooms, etc.

Location – The location in which we communicate influences the manner and nature of communication. Communication done from a podium to a vast audience needs to be loud. The same form of communication cannot be done in a meeting room. The actual location of the office space communicates status. An office located in the business district of a city conveys greater success in business when compared to one located in the suburbs.

Distance – The physical distance between the people communicating influences the nature of communication. Virtual offices or communicating with long-distance partners requires different forms of communication like telephone messages, video- conferencing, e-mail, etc. We have discussed the two broad types of communication – verbal and non-verbal- in detail.
