modules.title: Communication Models
text: Communication models are simplified representations that explain how communication takes place between individuals or groups. They help in understanding the basic elements of the communication process and the relationship between these elements. By presenting communication in a structured form, these models make it easier to analyse how messages are created, transmitted, and interpreted.

Most communication models include key components such as the sender, message, channel, receiver, and feedback. The sender is the person who initiates the communication by expressing an idea or information. This idea is organised into a message and transmitted through a channel, such as speech, writing, or digital media. The receiver is the person who receives and interprets the message. Feedback is the response given by the receiver, which indicates whether the message has been understood correctly. For example, during a business meeting, a manager may explain a new policy to employees, and the employees may ask questions or provide responses as feedback.

Several scholars have developed models to explain communication. The Shannon–Weaver Model of Communication focuses on the transmission of messages through channels, while the SMCR Model of Communication, proposed by David K. Berlo, explains communication through the elements of source, message, channel, and receiver. These models help in understanding communication more clearly and improving communication practices in academic and professional contexts.

David Berlo’s Model of Communication, commonly known as the SMCR Model, was proposed by communication theorist David K. Berlo in 1960. The model explains communication as a systematic process involving four major components: Source, Message, Channel, and Receiver (SMCR). Berlo emphasised that effective communication depends on how these components interact and on the abilities and characteristics of both the sender and the receiver.
David Berlo’s Model of Communication: Flowchart Representation
Source (Sender) ↓ Message ↓ Channel ↓ Receiver Components of the SMCR Model.
David Berlo’s Model of Communication: Flowchart Representation

Source (Sender) The source is the individual or organisation that initiates the communication by sending a message. According to Berlo, the effectiveness of communication largely depends on the sender’s communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, and cultural background. A manager explaining company policies during a meeting, for instance, acts as the source of communication. If the manager communicates clearly and understands the audience, the message becomes more effective.
David Berlo’s Model of Communication: Flowchart Representation

Message The message refers to the information, idea, or feeling that the sender intends to convey. It includes elements such as content, structure, code, and treatment. Content refers to the actual information being shared, while structure refers to the way the message is organised. For example, a business presentation explaining a new marketing strategy contains structured information supported by charts and examples to make the message understandable.
David Berlo’s Model of Communication: Flowchart Representation

Channel The channel is the medium through which the message travels from the sender to the receiver. Berlo highlighted the importance of sensory channels such as hearing, seeing, touching, smelling, and tasting. In business communication, common channels include meetings, emails, telephone calls, reports, and digital platforms. For instance, a company announcing a new product through a video presentation uses visual and auditory channels.
David Berlo’s Model of Communication: Flowchart Representation

Receiver The receiver is the individual or group that interprets and understands the message. Similar to the source, the receiver’s communication skills, knowledge, attitudes, and cultural context influence how the message is interpreted. For example, employees listening to a training session may interpret the message differently depending on their experience and understanding. Overall, Berlo’s SMCR model highlights that communication is effective only when the sender and receiver share a similar understanding and when the message is transmitted through appropriate channels.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

Shannon and Weaver (1949) devised a visual model of a communication system for use with electronic media, known as the Shannon and Weaver model of communication or the "Mathematical model of communication.".
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

This model includes a source of information that generates the desired message from a set of possible messages, such as written or spoken words, visuals, music, etc. We can refer to the sender as a communicator, speaker, or message source. The sender chooses which messages to deliver, how to handle them, and which channel to use so that his or her intended audience may receive and follow them.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

A transmitter converts this message into signals suitable for transmission from a set of possible messages, such as written or spoken words, pictures, music, and so on. A channel is a path through which signals from the transmitter are transmitted to the receiver. A receiver, which acts as an inverse transmitter, converts the sent signals into a message, and A destination is the message's end consumer. The model identifies three levels of challenges in information communication: A. Technical - issues with the reliability of transferring information from the sender to the receiver via signals. B. Semantic - issues involving the receiver's interpretation of meaning as the sender's intended meaning. C. Influential - problems about the success with which meanings are transferred to the recipient, as well as the receiver's following desired behaviour. While transmitting signals, unwanted distractions such as sound (in the case of radio) or telephone noise (in the case of telephone) are likely to be added. This model tries to describe how to overcome noise and how much redundancy is required for the receiver to receive the signal, i.e., the correct messages.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

Shannon and Weaver's model is primarily concerned with technical, semantic, and effective communication issues. We can learn from this model that by considering the following factors, we may reduce uncertainty and minimise the effects of noise: the sender's ability to encode and the receiver's ability to decode messages.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

Even though the model aims to explain the communication process in greater detail, it is a linear, one-way communication model that places little focus on feedback. Communication is represented in this model as a one-way, linear process.
Shannon and Weaver Model of Communication

Shannon and Weaver distinguish between source and transmitter and receiver and destination. They imply that the transmitting end has two roles and the receiving end has two. Noise: Any unwanted sound or disturbance that enters the channel that is beyond the control of the transmitter or receiver is referred to as noise. Reduced noise, higher bandwidth, and enhanced signal strength can all improve the efficiency of a communication system.

modules.title: Barriers To Communication
text: Communication fails when the message received is not identical to the message that is sent. Several factors could interfere with the exchange of messages.
‘Noise’ refers to all these factors that disrupt communication and can be classified under the following types:
Physical noise – Distracting sounds, poor acoustics, or just information overload could interfere with the listening process.
Physiological noise – Hearing or other disabilities, fatigue, or physical illness could come in the way of both speaking and listening.

Environmental barriers – An environmental barrier is the same as physical noise, which could be in the form of distracting sounds, an overcrowded room, poor facilities and acoustics, all of which may hinder the ability to listen to and understand the message.

Individual barriers – A major barrier to interpersonal communication is a tendency to judge, evaluate, approve, or disapprove of the views of another person. This happens particularly in situations where we have strong feelings about something. In such cases, we tend to block out communication and form our own viewpoints.

Organisational barriers – In organisations that are too hierarchical, that is, where there are multiple ‘layers’, messages may have to pass through many levels before they finally reach the receiver. Each level may add to, modify or completely change the message, so much so that it becomes distorted by the time it reaches the intended receiver. In other words, there is likely to be a loss of meaning and the message may not reach the receiver in the same way as it was intended by the sender. The following example illustrates an organisational barrier to communication. The Chief of the Space Centre gets to know about the possibility of seeing Halley’s Comet and decides that the entire organisation should witness this spectacle. He sends the following memo to the Director. Tomorrow evening, at 20:00 hours, we will be able to see Halley’s Comet in the sky through the naked eye. Since this is not an everyday event, everyone at the Centre should assemble outside in their best clothes to watch it. If it rains, we will not be able to see it very well, in which case everyone should assemble in the Canteen. The Director then sends the following memo to various Executive Directors: By order of the Chief, we will be able to see ‘Halley’s Comet’ at 20:00 hrs, tomorrow evening. If it is raining, we shall not be able to see it very well on site, in our best clothes. In that case, the disappearance of the Comet will be followed through in the Canteen. This is something which we cannot see happening everyday. The Executive Director sends out memos to the Heads of Departments as follows: By order of the Chief, we shall follow through, in our best clothes, the disappearance of the Comet in the Canteen at 20:00 hrs, tomorrow evening. The Chief will tell us whether it is going to rain. This is something which we cannot see happening everyday. The Heads of Departments send the following message to their managers: If it is raining in the Canteen tomorrow evening, which is something we cannot see happening every day, our Chief in his best clothes will disappear at 20:00 hrs. Finally, each Manager sends the following notice to their Executives: Tomorrow evening, at 20:00 hrs. our Chief will disappear. It is a pity that we cannot see this happening every day. As you can see, by the time the message is passed down from the Chief to the lower-level executives, it is distorted completely, to the extent that the original message is interpreted differently by each level in the organisation. Another type of organisational barrier is a ‘departmental barrier’. This means that each department in an organisation function in isolation and there is no coordination or communication between them.

Channel barriers – In the earlier section, it was pointed out that communication can fail due to any of the different elements going wrong. Wrong choice of channel is one of the main barriers to communication. Using the wrong medium of advertising, or conveying a message orally when a written letter would be more appropriate, are examples. The written channel is more appropriate when the communication is more formal or for keeping things on record, while emotional messages such as feelings about co-workers are better conveyed orally.

Linguistic and cultural barriers – When the sender of the message uses a language that the receiver does not understand, the communication will not succeed. Either the sender may be using a different or foreign language, or the language used may be too highly technical for the receiver to understand, Linguistic barriers may also occur in cross-cultural advertising and distort communication when translating campaigns or slogans literally from one language to another. For example, Pepsi’s slogan “Come Alive with Pepsi”, when translated into Chinese, reads “Pepsi brings your ancestors back from the grave!”. Cultural differences refer to differences in values and perceptions, which may affect the interpretation of the message by the receiver. For example, a joke about women may be taken in the wrong sense if the receiver belongs to a culture in which women are highly respected.

Semantic barriers – The word ‘semantics refers to the meaning of words and the way in which they are used. For example, different words may have different meanings in different cultures. Failure to take this into consideration could lead to serious blunders. Example – Saying ‘The new product launch went like a bomb’ in British English would mean that the new product launch was a success. On the other hand, saying ‘The product launch bombed’ in American English would mean that the new product was a disaster.

Non-verbal barriers – This refers to the non-verbal communication that goes with a particular message. Non-verbal communication includes tone of voice, body language such as gestures and facial expressions, etc. If the tone of voice and body language is negative, the communication will fail, however positive the spoken and written message. For example, if you happen to meet a long-lost friend and say “I am delighted to meet you”, but in a sad tone of voice, the exact opposite message will be conveyed. Therefore, it is important to avoid giving conflicting signals, through the use of non-verbal communication.

modules.title: Business Communication: Concept And Importance
text: Business communication refers to the exchange of information, ideas, and messages within and outside an organisation to achieve professional and organisational objectives. In contemporary organisations, communication is not merely a supportive function but a central process that shapes coordination, decision-making, and relationships among employees, managers, stakeholders, and customers. Whether it takes the form of emails, reports, meetings, presentations, or digital messaging, business communication enables individuals to share knowledge, clarify tasks, and ensure that organisational activities proceed efficiently.

Modern workplaces operate in dynamic environments characterised by technological advancement, globalisation, and multicultural teams. In such contexts, effective communication becomes essential for aligning organisational goals with employee actions. Managers must communicate policies and strategies clearly, employees must report progress and challenges, and organisations must maintain transparent communication with clients, investors, and the public. For instance, a project manager coordinating a software development team relies on clear instructions, progress reports, and regular meetings to ensure that all team members understand their responsibilities and deadlines.

Business communication also contributes to building professional relationships and organisational culture. When communication is open, respectful, and structured, it fosters trust, collaboration, and mutual understanding among employees. Conversely, poor communication can lead to misunderstandings, delays, and workplace conflicts. In service- oriented industries such as banking, healthcare, and hospitality, communication with customers directly affects satisfaction and organisational reputation.

In the digital era, business communication extends beyond traditional face-to-face interactions to include virtual meetings, collaborative platforms, and social media engagement. These tools enable organisations to operate across geographical boundaries while maintaining constant communication. Thus, understanding the principles and practices of business communication is fundamental for individuals seeking to function effectively in professional environments.

The concept of business communication encompasses the systematic process through which information is created, transmitted, received, and interpreted within a business environment. It involves the purposeful exchange of messages among individuals or groups to accomplish organisational objectives such as coordination, decision-making, problem- solving, and relationship management. Unlike casual conversation, business communication is goal-oriented, structured, and aligned with professional norms.

Business communication includes both internal communication and external communication. Internal communication occurs within an organisation among employees, departments, and management. For example, a human resources department sending a circular about workplace policies to employees represents internal communication. External communication, on the other hand, occurs between the organisation and external stakeholders such as customers, suppliers, investors, and the public. An advertisement announcing a new product or a company responding to customer feedback on social media illustrates external communication.

The concept also incorporates multiple communication channels and forms. These include oral communication such as meetings, presentations, and discussions; written communication such as emails, reports, and memos; and visual communication through charts, infographics, and presentations. In digital workplaces, collaborative tools such as video conferencing and instant messaging platforms further expand communication possibilities.
Thus, business communication represents a structured and strategic exchange of information designed to facilitate organisational functioning and professional interaction.

Business communication plays a crucial role in ensuring the smooth functioning and growth of organisations. It enables employees and management to share information effectively, coordinate tasks, and achieve organisational goals. When communication is clear and systematic, employees understand their roles and responsibilities, reducing confusion and improving productivity. For instance, detailed project instructions provided by a team leader help employees complete tasks efficiently and within deadlines.

Another important aspect of business communication is decision-making. Managers rely on accurate information, feedback, and reports to analyse situations and make informed decisions. Without effective communication channels, vital information may not reach decision-makers in time, potentially affecting organisational performance.

Business communication also helps in building professional relationships. Transparent communication between managers and employees encourages trust and cooperation. Similarly, clear communication with customers and business partners strengthens organisational credibility and long-term partnerships. For example, timely responses to customer inquiries and complaints demonstrate professionalism and commitment to service quality.

In addition, effective communication contributes to conflict management and problem- solving within organisations. When employees openly discuss issues and share perspectives, misunderstandings can be resolved before they escalate into larger conflicts.

Finally, business communication supports organisational reputation and brand image. The way an organisation communicates through advertisements, press releases, or social media interactions shapes public perception. Therefore, effective communication is essential for maintaining trust, credibility, and a positive organisational identity.

modules.title: Corporate Communication In Organisations
text: Business communication is diverse and involves both ‘internal stakeholders’ within the organisation, as well as ‘external stakeholders’ outside the organisation. A manager has to constantly communicate with and maintain good relations with each of these stakeholders or public. This will enable the organisation to achieve its overall goals and project a favourable image.

Managers have to stay in continuous touch with their internal stakeholders like their superiors, peers, subordinates, shareholders, employees and unions. At the same time managers have to communicate with external stakeholders such as customers, intermediaries (distributors and retailers), suppliers of materials and components, government, bankers, society at large and the media. Effective business communication therefore involves both internal as well as external communication. We will now look at some of the reasons for communication with internal and external stakeholders, as well as the appropriate channels to be used in each case.
Internal business communication is the exchange of information within a company. It involves interaction with the following stakeholders:
Shareholders Let us now discuss the communication involved with these internal stakeholders.

Every organisation has a formal reporting system. Superiors are the higher ups in the organisation to whom you report. The frequency of interaction with them will vary, depending on your position and responsibilities, as well as their need for information. As a salesperson, you may have to submit daily or weekly reports of sales progress. As a marketing manager, you may be required to make periodic presentations on marketing strategy for new product launches to the Vice President, Marketing. Occasionally, you may also approach your superiors to communicate your feelings about your job, unsolved problems with co-workers and your suggestions for improvement of the organisation.

Communication with superiors could be through written channels, such as reports, or through oral face-to-face channels, such as presentations and one-to-one meetings. When trying to solve problems or improve relationships, oral face-to-face channels are most effective, as explained in the previous unit.

Peers are your co-workers, or people at the same level within an organisation. For example, a marketing manager and an HR manager are peers, since they work at the same level within different departments. Communication between peers is essential for functional coordination. An Advertising Manager for example, will need to communicate with the Finance Manager regarding approval of the advertising budget for a new product launch. Information sharing is another reason for communication between peers.

The Advertising Manager and the Sales Manager in the Marketing Department may need to communicate regarding the special features of a product to be highlighted in an advertising campaign. Regular communication between co-workers in different departments is also essential to ensure that they work together as a team to achieve the common goals of the organisation.
The most appropriate channel of communication between peers is the oral face-to-face channel, since it helps to build good rapport and improves work relationships.

Subordinates are people in the organisation who work below you or report directly to you. For example, as the Marketing Manager, you may have Assistant Managers reporting to you, who in turn may have Marketing Executives reporting to them. The most common reason for communication with subordinates is to convey organisational procedures, policies, targets and goals. Other reasons include performance appraisal and feedback, reward and recognition aspects and disciplinary issues.

Appropriate channels of communication with subordinates may be both oral and written, depending on the situation. Communicating about organisational procedures is best done through written communication. But, performance appraisal and feedback should be done through an oral one-to one meeting and discussion.

Employees/unions can be quite powerful. Therefore communication with them is essential. The reasons for communication include welfare aspects, disciplinary aspects and terms of employment. All these should be clearly spelt out and kept on record. Hence written channels such as written contracts are the most appropriate channels.

Shareholders are very important internal stakeholders, since they are the owners of the company. Therefore, it is essential to be completely transparent with shareholders and to keep them informed of all developments in the company. It is essential to communicate with shareholders to keeping them informed about the following:
New projects undertaken by the company.
Any major problems faced by the company.

The steps being taken to tackle the major problems This is part of public relations, through which the company projects a positive image of itself in the eyes of shareholders. The appropriate channels of communication with shareholders include oral and written channels. Communication with the shareholder is done through:
Superiors - Written reports; Presentations; Meetings; Awareness of progress; Suggestions and feedback; Problem solving.
Peers - Face-to-face meetings; Overall Objective: Coordination; Teamwork;.
Subordinates - Written communication; Face-to-face meetings; Compliance with instructions and policies; Review of work progress; Feedback.
Employees/Unions - Written communication; Overall Objective: Employee satisfaction and.
Shareholders - Meetings; Advertisements; Brochures; Building trust and confidence.

Before we discuss the reasons for communication with external stakeholders, it is important that you understand the overall importance of external business communication. External business communication is essential to:
Enhance credit rating Let us now examine the reasons which make external business communication essential.

For successful marketing, organisations need to inform and create awareness among consumers about their existing and new products. This is largely done through advertising, which is a form of mass communication. This is very much a part of external business communication.

Today, organisations need to focus on projecting themselves as responsible corporate and social citizens. This is known as corporate social responsibility. For example, they need to communicate the fact that they are involved in social development or in environmental protection. This involves being in touch with various external stakeholders, especially consumers, media and the society at large.

When customers have a positive image of the company, the company’s share value will increase and the shareholders’ wealth increases, thereby enhancing shareholder value. Shareholder confidence in the company also drives shareholder value. When shareholder value increases, they will participate in the company’s expansion and growth.
Sometimes when a company is facing a crisis, a public relations campaign may be needed to:
Put things in a proper perspective.

Restore the image of the company in the eyes of consumers, the media and society Public relations require effective communication with various external stakeholders. For example, a few years ago, Reliance was prosecuted by the government for irregularities in the stock market. Shareholders lost confidence in the company. Reliance then mounted a counter campaign against the government, where they told the truth, gave the facts and figures and denied the allegations made against them. This helped them to regain lost confidence and salvage their image. Similarly, when Coke and Pepsi were accused of pesticides in their soft drinks, they had to undertake a massive public relations exercise to set right their image in the eyes of the public.

An organisation’s credit rating will also go up if it maintains good external communication. This way its borrowing ability will increase. The organisation can also raise more money for expansion and growth.

Having emphasised the importance of external business communication, let us now go into the reasons for communicating with external stakeholders and the channels used to communicate with them, just as we did with internal communication.
External business communication involves interaction with the following stakeholders:
Media Let us briefly discuss the business communication done with these stakeholders.
Organisations need to communicate with consumers to provide information about:

New product developments Organisations also need to redress consumer complaints, so as to maintain consumer preference and confidence in their brands. The written channel is the most appropriate medium for communicating with consumers. This could take the form of letters, or mass media advertising.
Intermediaries refer to the trade – distributors, wholesalers, retailers, franchisees, etc. It is necessary to communicate with them to provide information about:

Merchandising or the visual display of products Keeping intermediaries aware and informed and motivating them to meet targets through competitions, prizes and incentives is extremely important for the success of any product. The appropriate channels of communication with intermediaries could be both oral and written channels. Some examples of written channels are:
Advertisements announcing special offers and incentives.
Dealer newsletters inviting dealers to share their experiences Some examples of oral channels are:

These are suppliers of raw material, components, power, water or other utilities. Communication with suppliers is essential to give technical specifications, ensure quality and timely delivery. Today, due to ‘outsourcing’ or relying on outside sources for raw materials and components, there is need for more sophisticated and direct communication and a more continuous, on-going relationship with suppliers. The Internet now plays an important role in communication with suppliers in ‘Business to Business’ (B2B) communication.

Many organisations today enter into a partnership with their suppliers, whereby there is total involvement on both sides. For example, a company engineer might train the shop floor technical staff of a supplier of automotive components, in order to improve the quality of the components. The supplier may suggest a change in the company’s specification process.

Direct, one-to-one communication is required with suppliers to ensure transparency and clarity, with respect to specifications. The oral face-to-face channel is most appropriate, although the online channel is being increasingly used in supplier communication.

Communicating with the government is particularly important in the Indian context and is a part of public relations. Many Indian companies even appoint a PR officer for maintaining good relations with the government. The reasons for communicating with the government include compliance with tax matters and legal aspects, seeking clearances for new activities such as joint ventures, borrowing from overseas banks, foreign exchange requirements, etc.

Communication with the government could take place through both oral and written channels. Periodic meetings may be held with regard to statutory compliances such as licensing. However, most of the time, written communication through formal letters is more appropriate. This is because clearances for various activities have to be sought in writing.

As pointed out earlier, organisations need to communicate with the community at large to project themselves as responsible corporate citizens. ‘Corporate social responsibility’ as it is called, is top priority with many organisations today. Some of the ways in which companies are participating in social development are:

Ensuring that they do not pollute the environment Organisations communicate these measures to the society. The channels of communication with society could be oral and direct – for example, talking to elders in a village or locality, about family planning or schools for children. Mass media advertising in the form of ‘public service advertising’ could also be used to spread these social service messages. For example, United Breweries ran a public service campaign with the caption ‘Drinking and driving don’t mix’, to spread the message of avoiding drunken driving. There is a large element of public relations in communication with society.

Like shareholders, organisations need to communicate with bankers both in good times and bad times. The reasons for communicating with bankers are the same as those for shareholders. In addition, advance notice needs to be given to bankers regarding any dislocation in repayment schedules and justification has to be provided for any additional fund needs. The overall purpose is to build rapport with the bank, so as to increase borrowing ability.

Communication with bankers could take place through oral channels – for example, periodic meetings with the Finance Manager of the company to keep them informed of stock build up trends, or future trends that could affect working capital needs. Special meetings may also be held to keep them posted about expansion, contraction and diversification plans, lockouts, strikes and anything else that may affect cash flow.

In addition to oral channels, periodic written reports need to be submitted to the bank on overall business conditions. Transparency is needed in dealings with the bank and failure to keep them informed could lead to the company’s collapse.
For example, the Enron Company did not communicate with their shareholders and bankers about the difficult times that they were going through. This ultimately led to the company’s ruin.

Today, the media are becoming more powerful and investigative. They are intruding into people’s personal lives. If wrongly informed, the media can destroy an institution. Therefore, the primary reason for an organisation to communicate with the media is to maintain good relations. If the company projects a favourable image to the media, the media in turn will carry a positive story about the company for free. This is known as ‘publicity’ and is part of public relations.

For example, a press release in a newspaper may highlight some of the achievements or awards won by the company. This type of publicity is highly credible and can have a powerful influence on public opinion.
Communication with the media takes place through both oral channels such as press conferences, as well as written channels such as letters and news releases.

modules.title: Formal Communication Networks in Organisations
text: A communication network refers to how information flows within an organisation. Information inside a company does not just float around randomly; it flows through a managed, regulated, and structured system.

Adler's Definition: "Communication networks are regular patterns of person-to-person relationships through which information flows in an organisation." Communication networks are broadly divided into two types: Formal Communication Networks and Informal Communication Networks (Grapevine).

Intranet: A secure, private internal digital workspace used to connect employees, centralise company information, and streamline communication. Authoritarian: Encouraging or demanding strict obedience to authority while ignoring others' opinions.
Ego Clashes: Arguments or disagreements between people of equal status or similar position.

Conduit: A channel or central person through whom information passes. Egalitarian: Equal and unrestricted, where everyone has an equal voice. Double Negative: A grammatical mistake where two negative words in the same sentence cancel each other out and accidentally create a positive meaning.
Follows the official authority chain and is limited to task-related communication. Uses official channels such as memos, bulletins, notices, and the company intranet.

Horizontal (Lateral) - Direction & Examples: Co-workers at the same level in; Main Reasons: Coordinating tasks, sharing; Key Benefits: Fosters strong teamwork toward; Key Disadvantages / Challenges: Potential for ego clashes and.

Communication - Direction & Examples: same or different departments; Main Reasons: goals, resolving interpersonal/; Key Benefits: common organisational goals; Key Disadvantages / Challenges: conflicts among equal-level co-.

Diagonal Communication - Direction & Examples: Hybrid of vertical & horizontal:; Main Reasons: Cross-departmental; Key Benefits: Breaks down silos, skips slow; Key Disadvantages / Challenges: Hesitation to speak up; bypasses.
Keep direct supervisors informed even when communicating directly across departments. Summarise decisions and share them with everyone affected so no team member is left out of the loop.
Use active listening (summarise points, ask clarifying questions, recap action items) and avoid departmental jargon.
Prioritise transparency by using channels that create an easily accessible written record.

modules.title: Informal Communication, Other Networks & Common Mistakes
text: Also known as the "Grapevine." Does NOT follow any fixed direction or official channels (memos, notices, bulletin boards). Moves freely in any direction, skips authority levels, and often happens outside work (company picnics, parties, carpools) based on friendship and shared personal or career interests.
Satisfies employees' social needs while assisting in task accomplishment.
Fills transparency gaps left by formal channels—especially during crises like strikes or layoffs before official announcements are released.
Helps confirm important organisational news (such as a major acquisition).
Can be used constructively by management to test reactions before making official announcements (e.g., floating a proposal informally to gauge staff reaction).

Speed: Information spreads very rapidly by bypassing formal channels. Informal Updates: Management can use it to quickly share informal updates. Verification: Both managers and employees can use it to verify the accuracy of information.
Cost-effective: It is entirely free and spontaneous.
Emotional Outlet: Gives employees a safe outlet to express anxieties and opinions without fear.

Managerial Rule: Do NOT try to suppress the grapevine, and NEVER use it to threaten employees. Accept it while countering false rumours by sharing both positive and negative news openly through formal channels. Both formal and informal networks must co-exist.

Chain Network - How Information Flows: Flows strictly up and down the formal hierarchy; each person talks only to the person directly above or below; Centralisation & Key Feature: Fairly centralised; rigidly follows chain of command; middle person controls messages.

Y Network - How Information Flows: Resembles an upside-down "Y"; flows up and down and branches out to employees reporting to a supervisor; Centralisation & Key Feature: Fairly centralised; person at the fork of the "Y" acts as the central controller.

Wheel Network - How Information Flows: All information flows to and from one single central person (the hub/leader); members rarely talk to each other; Centralisation & Key Feature: Most centralised; very fast and efficient for getting information out directly through the leader.

Circle Network - How Information Flows: Each member communicates only with the two adjoining neighbours on either side; Centralisation & Key Feature: Decentralised; freer communication among immediate neighbours, but not across the whole group.

All-Channel (Star) Network - How Information Flows: Flows upward, downward, and laterally freely among ALL group members; Centralisation & Key Feature: Most decentralised; supports an egalitarian, participative culture and highest member satisfaction.
Rule: Using two negative words in the same sentence cancels them out and creates an unintended positive meaning.

For example, Incorrect: "You cannot be trusted with the job as you do not have no experience." (Implies you DO have experience!) Correct: "You cannot be trusted with the job as you do not have any experience.".
Incorrect: "I couldn't hardly understand what she said." Correct: "I could hardly understand what she said." (or "I couldn't understand what she said.").
Incorrect: "This attitude will not get you nowhere." Correct: "This attitude will not get you anywhere." (or "This attitude will get you nowhere.").
Incorrect: "The new financial initiatives may not last hardly a month." Correct: "The new financial initiatives may hardly last a month." (or "The new financial initiatives may not last a month.").

modules.title: Role of Communication in Business Decision Making
text: Business decision-making is continuous and rarely done by one person alone—it is a collective outcome shaped by discussions, data, and feedback. Communication is the backbone of decision- making because it connects people, processes, and information so the right data reaches the right people at the right time.

Information Sharing and Accuracy: Sound decisions rely on accurate data shared through reports, emails, and meetings (e.g., gathering inputs from market research, finance, and production before launching a product).

Supporting Managerial Functions: Planning: Gathering insights to set realistic goals; Organising: Assigning tasks and defining responsibilities clearly; Controlling: Giving feedback to review performance and adjust strategies.

Role of Communication Flows: Upward: Shares operational problems and bottom-up suggestions; Downward: Conveys executive decisions, policies, and operational instructions; Horizontal: Coordinates across functions (e.g., Marketing obtaining budget approval from Finance).
Enhancing Collaboration and Problem Solving: Open idea-sharing across multidisciplinary teams produces more inclusive, innovative, and higher-quality decisions.
Role of Informal Insights: Helps management gauge employee sentiments before major structural changes (must be verified via formal channels).
Speed and Timeliness: Modern digital tools enable rapid responses during critical emergencies, such as supply chain disruptions.

modules.title: Listening – Process, Classification, and Barriers
text: Overview and Four-Step Process of Listening
Lundsteen's Definition: "Listening is a highly complex process by which spoken language is converted to meaning in the mind.".
Overview and Four-Step Process of Listening
Stephen Covey identified listening as a core habit of highly effective individuals— emphasising that it is an intentional skill requiring active practice.
Overview and Four-Step Process of Listening
Hearing vs. Listening: Hearing is a passive physiological mechanism; Listening is an active cognitive process requiring concentration, decoding, contextual evaluation, and synthesis.
Overview and Four-Step Process of Listening

Four Steps of the Listening Process: a; Hearing: Receiving auditory signals through physical attention. b; Interpreting: Decoding speech patterns using personal knowledge, context, and non-verbal cues. c; Evaluating: Assessing the validity, relevance, and implications of the received message. d; Responding: Offering verbal or non-verbal feedback to confirm comprehension.

Discriminative - Purpose & Mechanics: Distinguishing basic acoustic differences and vocal cues (the foundation of listening); Context & Application: Essential for language acquisition and voice recognition.

Comprehensive - Purpose & Mechanics: Synthesising vocabulary, grammar, and non-verbal signals to understand explicit message meaning; Context & Application: Attending lectures, instructions, and routine work briefings.

Evaluative - Purpose & Mechanics: Critically analyzing message validity, logic, and intent to render judgment; Context & Application: Evaluating sales presentations, negotiations, or persuasive speeches.

Appreciative - Purpose & Mechanics: Engaging with spoken content for aesthetic enjoyment or personal satisfaction; Context & Application: Listening to music, artistic poetry, or inspiring keynote speeches.

Empathetic - Purpose & Mechanics: Understanding the speaker's emotional state, perspective, and underlying feelings without judgment; Context & Application: Customer support resolutions, personal feedback sessions.

Therapeutic - Purpose & Mechanics: Providing a supportive environment to help the speaker process issues and discover solutions; Context & Application: Counseling settings, structured performance recovery sessions.

Dialogic (Relational) - Purpose & Mechanics: Collaborative exchange where understanding is iteratively built through mutual dialogue; Context & Application: Team brainstorming, peer mentoring, joint problem- solving.
Research indicates that top-level organizational communication can lose up to 80% of its intent by the time it reaches frontline workers due to listening barriers.
Physical: External distractions including environmental noise, poor room ventilation, uncomfortable seating, or constant phone notifications during meetings.
Attitudinal: Personal preoccupation, bias against the speaker, or Egocentrism (the belief that one already possesses full knowledge, closing off input).

Wrong Assumptions: Believing communication is solely the speaker's burden, viewing listening as passive, or assuming speakers hold all positional authority; David J; Schwartz: "Big people monopolise the listening; Small people monopolise the talking.".
Cultural: Regional accent variations, idioms, and divergent cultural norms (e.g., Eastern traditions often value silent reflection, whereas Western contexts emphasize immediate verbal response).
Gender: Differing perceptual focus: research suggests men frequently listen for functional facts, whereas women often process.
Lack of Training: Treating listening as an innate trait rather than a professional capability requiring instruction (pioneered by leaders like Lee Iacocca at Chrysler).
Bad Listening Habits: Simulating attention, attempting to memorize every isolated fact rather than core themes, or tuning out complex subject matter prematurely.

modules.title: Improving Listening & Listening in a Business Context
text: Create a Conducive Environment: Neutralize ambient noise, adjust physical comfort settings, and eliminate digital interruptions.
Select Face-to-Face Channels: Prioritize direct contact over voice-only channels to capture non-verbal cues and reduce misunderstandings.
Be Open-Minded & Avoid Distractions: Maintain intellectual curiosity and suspend pre-formed judgments about the speaker.
Use Non-Verbal Cues: Signal engagement using responsive eye contact, receptive posture, and appropriate head nods.
Use Verbal Cues: Provide constructive feedback, seek clarifying details, and paraphrase complex ideas to confirm alignment.
Listen First Before Responding: Avoid formulating counterarguments while the speaker is addressing you.
Use the Speaker-Listener Gap Constructively: Apply spare mental bandwidth to summarize key ideas, evaluate evidence, and outline logical connections.
Focus on Both Verbal & Non-Verbal Messages: Harmonize auditory speech with body language, voice inflection, and pacing.
Focus on Content Rather Than Delivery: Disregard minor speaker mannerisms, visual slide design, or vocal accent to evaluate core arguments.
Ask Questions of Yourself & Take Notes: Continuously evaluate the primary thesis, supporting data, and structural organization of the talk.
Do Not Be Judgmental: Maintain an objective stance, encourage full expression of ideas, and refrain from dismissing complex concerns.
